title: Implement the quick sort algorithm, explain the partition step and pivot choice, and analyse its time complexity.
keyPoints: Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions smaller-left and larger-right, then recursively sorts each side in place.
The partition step does the real work: it places the pivot in its final sorted position in one pass.
Average time is O(n log n); worst case is O(n^2) when pivots are consistently the smallest or largest element.
Median-of-three or random pivot selection makes the worst case astronomically unlikely.
Quick sort is in-place with O(log n) stack space; no merge step and no auxiliary array needed.
It is not stable: equal elements can be reordered during partitioning.
Java's Arrays.sort for primitives uses a dual-pivot quicksort variant for its cache-friendly, fast performance.

s1_definition.oneliner: Pick a pivot, partition smaller-left and larger-right, then recursively sort each side in place.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Quick sort** – a divide-and-conquer, comparison-based sorting algorithm that sorts in place.
- **Partition** – rearranges elements so everything smaller than the pivot is on the left, everything larger on the right, and the pivot is in its final position.
- **Recursion** – after partition, recursively sort the left and right parts; no merge step needed.
- **Pivot quality** – determines performance: balanced partitions give O(n log n), worst pivots give O(n^2).
- **Java usage** – `Arrays.sort` for primitives uses a dual-pivot quicksort for its speed and cache friendliness.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must sort a pile of transactions by amount. A clerk grabs one transaction as the pivot and splits the pile into smaller-than-pivot on the left and larger-than-pivot on the right, placing the pivot exactly between them where it now belongs forever. She then repeats the splitting on each sub-pile independently until every sub-pile has one item and the whole pile is sorted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that picks a pivot, partitions the array so everything smaller is on the left and everything larger is on the right, and then recursively sorts the two partitions. The partition step does the real work: it places the pivot in its final sorted position in a single pass. There is no merge step because the partitioning already arranges elements relative to each other.

The performance depends entirely on pivot quality. Balanced partitions give O(n log n), but consistently bad pivots (smallest or largest) degrade to O(n^2). Median-of-three or random pivot selection makes the worst case astronomically unlikely in practice.

Quick sort is in-place with O(log n) stack space and is cache-friendly with small constant factors, which is why it is often the fastest sort in practice. Java uses a dual-pivot quicksort for primitive arrays in `Arrays.sort`. However, it is not stable, so Java uses TimSort for object arrays where preserving the order of equal elements matters.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, quick sort is used for large in-memory arrays of transaction amounts when stability is not required and memory is tight. The pivot is chosen by median-of-three to avoid the worst case on nearly-sorted feeds.

Remember one sentence: quick sort partitions around a pivot in-place and recurses on both sides, averaging O(n log n) but needing a good pivot to avoid the rare quadratic worst case.
